args.text: --- title: 'Hello World' description: 'Change the FHE computation in the default template so that the E3 returns two times the sum, and run it again.' --- import { Callout, Steps } from 'nextra/components' import { Flow, LinkCard, LinkCards } from '@/components/ui' # Hello World This tutorial changes the FHE computation in the default template and runs the E3 again. It's for developers who've already done the [Quick Start](/build/quick-start). By the end, your E3 returns 2 × (a + b) instead of a + b, and you'll know which files hold the computation, its test, and its labels in the client. ## Before you begin You'll need the `my-first-e3` project from the [Quick Start](/build/quick-start), untouched. All paths on this page are relative to the project folder. ## How the template computes The FHE computation is one Rust function, `fhe_processor`, in `program/src/lib.rs`. The rest of the template just ferries ciphertexts to this function and carts its result off to the committee. 1. The client encrypts each number with the committee public key and calls `MyProgram.publishInput`. 2. When the input window closes, the coordination server (`server/index.ts`) reads the published inputs and sends them to the program server on port 13151. 3. The program server (`.interfold/support/dev/src/main.rs`) calls `fhe_processor` and sends the encrypted result back to the coordination server. 4. The coordination server publishes the encrypted result. The committee decrypts it. Here's the default computation in `program/src/lib.rs`. The doc comment above `policy` has been left out here: ```rust filename="program/src/lib.rs" use e3_compute_provider::{FHEProcessorInput, InputPolicy}; use fhe::bfv::Ciphertext; use fhe_traits::{DeserializeParametrized, Serialize}; pub fn policy() -> InputPolicy { InputPolicy::default() } /// Implementation of the CiphertextProcessor function pub fn fhe_processor(fhe_inputs: FHEProcessorInput<'_>) -> Vec { let mut sum = Ciphertext::zero(fhe_inputs.params); for (bytes, _) in fhe_inputs.ciphertexts { let ciphertext = Ciphertext::from_bytes(&bytes, fhe_inputs.params).unwrap(); sum += &ciphertext; } sum.to_bytes() } ``` - `FHEProcessorInput` has two fields. `ciphertexts` yields `(Vec, u64)` pairs one at a time: the serialized ciphertext and its input index. `params` holds the BFV parameters of the E3. - `Ciphertext::zero` makes the zero ciphertext, the start value. The `+=` operator adds each input ciphertext to it. This addition is homomorphic: the function adds the hidden values, but it can't see them. - `sum.to_bytes()` serializes the encrypted result. - `policy()` returns the input policy. The default policy uses every published input. The template requests E3s with the `insecure-512` parameter set. Its plaintext modulus is 100, so every result is calculated modulo 100. For this tutorial, 2 × (a + b) must be less than 100. ## Change the computation ### Stop the stack If `pnpm dev:all` is running, press `Ctrl+C` in its terminal. ### Double the encrypted sum In `program/src/lib.rs`, replace the `fhe_processor` function with this version: ```rust filename="program/src/lib.rs" {9-11} /// Implementation of the CiphertextProcessor function pub fn fhe_processor(fhe_inputs: FHEProcessorInput<'_>) -> Vec { let mut sum = Ciphertext::zero(fhe_inputs.params); for (bytes, _) in fhe_inputs.ciphertexts { let ciphertext = Ciphertext::from_bytes(&bytes, fhe_inputs.params).unwrap(); sum += &ciphertext; } // Add the encrypted sum to itself. The hidden value becomes 2 × (a + b). let doubled = &sum + ∑ doubled.to_bytes() } ``` `&sum + &sum` adds two ciphertexts and returns a new ciphertext. The function doesn't need any new imports. ### Update the unit test The test at the end of `program/src/lib.rs` encrypts 3 and 2 and calls `fhe_processor`. Change the expected value from 5 to 10: ```rust filename="program/src/lib.rs" let tally = Vec::::try_decode(&decrypted, Encoding::poly())?; assert_eq!(tally[0], 10); Ok(()) ``` ### Run the unit test ```bash cargo test -p e3-user-program ``` Cargo prints `test tests::test ... ok`. If the test fails, check your `fhe_processor` against the code in the previous step. ### Update the label on the input step In `client/src/pages/steps/EnterInputs.tsx`, find this line: ```tsx filename="client/src/pages/steps/EnterInputs.tsx" Ready to compute: {input1} + {input2} = ? ``` Change it to: ```tsx filename="client/src/pages/steps/EnterInputs.tsx" Ready to compute: 2 × ({input1} + {input2}) = ? ``` ### Update the label on the results step In `client/src/pages/steps/Results.tsx`, find this line: ```tsx filename="client/src/pages/steps/Results.tsx" { submittedInputs ? `${submittedInputs.input1} + ${submittedInputs.input2} = ${result !== null ? result : '…'}` : '…' } ``` Change it to: ```tsx filename="client/src/pages/steps/Results.tsx" { submittedInputs ? `2 × (${submittedInputs.input1} + ${submittedInputs.input2}) = ${result !== null ? result : '…'}` : '…' } ``` ### Start the stack ```bash pnpm dev:all ``` The `PROGRAM` process runs `interfold program start`. In dev mode, this command runs `cargo run --bin e3-support-scripts-dev`, so Cargo compiles the program server again with your new `fhe_processor`. ### Run an E3 Open [http://localhost:3000](http://localhost:3000). If the client's still showing the result of an earlier E3, select **Start over** in the top bar. Request an E3, then enter 5 and 3. The input step shows `Ready to compute: 2 × (5 + 3) = ?`. The results step shows `2 × (5 + 3) = 16`. ## Why nothing else changes - **The contract.** `MyProgram.publishInput` stores a commitment for each input, and `MyProgram.verify` checks the compute proof. Neither function has the computation in it. - **The coordination server.** `server/index.ts` sends every published input to the program server and publishes the output that it gets back. It's got no idea what the computation does. - **The deployment.** `pnpm dev:all` deploys the contracts again on a new local chain every time it starts. In dev mode, the program server runs `fhe_processor` without a proof, and the template deploys `MockOpenVmReceiptVerifier`, which accepts every receipt on the local chain. With real proofs, `MyProgram.verify` checks the OpenVM receipt against the `imageId` that `MyProgram` receives when it is deployed. Any change to the program changes that identity, so compile and deploy again. See [Compute provider](/build/e3-program/compute-provider). ## Update the integration test The template has an end-to-end test in `tests/integration.spec.ts`. It encrypts 1 and 2 and expects their sum. Once you've made your change, update the expected value: ```ts filename="tests/integration.spec.ts" expect(BigInt(result)).toBe(2n * (num1 + num2)) ``` Run the test with `pnpm test:integration`. This test needs a CLI that's built with the `test-only-skip-proof-aggregation` Cargo feature. Release binaries don't include it. See [Installation](/build/installation#install-the-cli) for a source build. ## Operations on ciphertexts The template uses the `fhe` crate from `gnosisguild/fhe.rs` at tag `v0.4.2`. For a `Ciphertext`, that crate implements these operators: | Operation | Operator | Example | | --------------------------- | -------------------- | ----------------- | | Add two ciphertexts | `+`, `+=` | `&a + &b` | | Subtract two ciphertexts | `-`, `-=` | `&a - &b` | | Negate a ciphertext | unary `-` | `-&a` | | Add or subtract a plaintext | `+`, `+=`, `-`, `-=` | `&a + &plaintext` | | Multiply by a plaintext | `*`, `*=` | `&a * &plaintext` | A `Plaintext` must use the same parameters object as the ciphertext, that is `fhe_inputs.params`. If the parameters objects don't match, the operator panics. All results wrap modulo the plaintext modulus. A negative result, for example from `&a - &b` with `a < b`, wraps to a large value. The crate also implements `*` for two ciphertexts. The default template doesn't use it, and this page doesn't cover it. ## Next steps Write the FHE computation for your own E3 program. Validate inputs and verify proofs in your E3 program contract. Find the file to edit for each part of the template.

declined.reason: Replaces the noun 'build' in 'a source build' (a term of art: compiling from source); it's a verb meaning to make roughly, wrong part of speech and wrong sense.

'a new ciphertext' / 'a new local chain' is the plain technical sense (a fresh value, a fresh chain); the technical genre allows no slang on terms of art, and the intensifier adds emphasis the original doesn't have.
